claims.text: Simultaneous high-scanning-rate DSC and in-situ HT-XRD can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across high-entropy alloys.
Directly correlating calorimetric signatures with real-time structural changes enables determination of the stated thermodynamic properties.
LPBF and arc melting can produce single-solid-solution high-entropy alloys.
The targeted initial alloys have a predominantly single-phase BCC structure.
The targeted alloys have homogeneous microstructures before melting.
Heating rates of 10–40 K/min in an inert atmosphere permit thermal transitions to be correlated with structural evolution during melting.
The approach is applicable when alloys show clear phase transitions and do not significantly phase-separate before melting.
HT-XRD can detect grain-boundary changes and evidence of elemental segregation during heating.
The detected microstructural evolution mediates the relationship between DSC-measured thermal-energy absorption and phase transitions.
Rapid heating produces clear and separable thermal events in complex high-entropy alloys.
HT-XRD captures structural changes corresponding to calorimetric events, including loss of crystallinity and phase transformations.
Combining DSC with HT-XRD reduces uncertainty caused by overlapping transitions in complex alloy systems.
The dual-technique approach can determine the thermodynamic properties with uncertainty near ±5%.
Conventional DSC-only measurements typically have uncertainties around or above 10% for these properties.
Overlapping transitions and unknown microstructural evolution limit the accuracy of conventional DSC-only measurements.
The approach works best for high-entropy alloys with uniform, single-phase microstructures.
Significant multiphase behavior or compositional inhomogeneity can obscure calorimetric or structural signatures and reduce the method's effectiveness.
The exact precision improvement and applicability across the entire high-entropy-alloy family remain unvalidated.
Failure to reduce uncertainty below 10%, or failure to establish a clear calorimetric-structural correlation, would falsify the approach.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis presents simultaneous DSC/HT-XRD as capable of determining volume change at melting, but the validation plan obtains volume change from complementary dilatometry, leaving unclear whether volume change is an output of the proposed dual-technique method itself.
